source: CBS Aruba, Fifth Population and Housing Census Aruba (2010), Table H-F.1 (n=34,845 housing units)
mapping_notes: Census reports only a connection rate: 93.4% of valid answers connected to the WEB piped/desalination network. Rubric rule 4 makes the 6.6% residual a CEILING on self-supply, and the census gives no description of what the residual households actually use, so no category can be allocated. Table H-D.3 does record rainwater tank / well use, but the census methodology notes (p.58) state that item covers water for plants and similar non-potable uses, NOT drinking, so it cannot be remapped to a main-drinking-source share (rubric rule 5/6 spirit). Left entirely null rather than guessing a split.
bounds_notes: Self-supply ceiling: <=6.6% of housing units for ALL four unpiped categories combined (2010). No drinking-specific question. 2020 census results not locatable online. Note Aruba's public supply is desalinated but network-distributed, which counts as piped per rubric and is therefore excluded from our columns.

source: Anguilla Statistics Department, Population and Housing Census 2011 – Selected Results, Table 20 'Source of drinking water' (n=4,935 households)
mapping_notes: Filled from the DRINKING-water table per rubric rule 1, not the household-supply table. Table 20: Bottled water 60.7% -> Packaged; Cistern piped into dwelling 32.4% + Cistern not piped 3.5% = 35.9% -> OtherUnpiped (a private rainwater cistern piped into the dwelling is still rainwater as a SOURCE — JMP 'piped' means piped from a network, so the delivery method does not move it out of our columns); Public well/tank 1.0% -> Borehole (well type not stated, so this could equally be a dug well/OtherUnpiped, but at 1.0% the choice is immaterial); Public piped 1.9% -> piped, excluded; Other (reverse osmosis / filtration) 2.0% left unallocated. Delivered set to 0 because neither census table offers a tanker/truck option and the categories account for the full sample — but see bounds_notes, trucked cistern refilling is masked. Single stratum, territory-wide values applied to both URBAN and RURAL. Household-supply table (for reference, NOT used for the fill): Cistern piped into dwelling 73.1%, Cistern not piped 5.8% (= 78.9% cisterns), Public piped into dwelling 15.3%, Public piped to yard 1.7%, Public standpipe 0.2%, Public well/tank 0.7%, Bottled 0.2%, Other 2.7%. The contrast is the classic island pattern: cisterns for household use, bottled for drinking.
bounds_notes: Drinking table as transcribed sums to 101.5% (60.7+32.4+3.5+1.9+1.0+2.0), i.e. ~1.5pp of rounding/overlap in the published rounding — below the ~102 threshold so not flagged, but the filled values should be treated as +/- ~1pp. Delivered is a known blind spot: cistern refilling by water truck is common practice in Anguilla and would be recorded inside the cistern categories, so the true Delivered share is >0 and is embedded in the 35.9% OtherUnpiped. Also available: breakdown by 14 districts (Table 19), which could support a within-territory split if ever needed.

source: Govern d'Andorra, 'Les aigues subterranies' (page blocked/JS-rendered, could not extract); only World Bank/JMP-family aggregates available (100% basic, ~90-91% safely managed)
mapping_notes: Not fillable. No connection-rate or source-of-water statistic was located. The only quantitative context found is that domestic use is 85% of total water consumption at 212 L/person/day (2025 press coverage), which says nothing about source category. JMP-family aggregates are modelled indicators and cannot resolve source type. Note AND is one of the territories dropped by drop_small_island_nations but a row is produced per rubric rule 10.
bounds_notes: Domestic consumption 85% of total water use, 212 L/person/day (2025) - consumption volume, not a source breakdown.

source: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census of Population and Housing (Island Areas), table HBG51 'Source of Water', DECENNIALAS2010, geography 0400000US60 (n=9,688 occupied housing units). Counts pulled directly from the Census API 2026-08-07.
mapping_notes: Full table: public system only 8,138 = 84.00%; public system AND catchment 432 = 4.46%; village water system only 962 = 9.93%; individual well 48 = 0.50%; catchment/tanks/drums only 46 = 0.47%; some other source (standpipe, spring, river, creek, etc.) 62 = 0.64%. Sums to 100.00. EXCLUDED as piped: public-only 84.00 + village system only 9.93 (village systems are piped community supply) = 93.93. HYBRID DECISION: 'public system and catchment' 4.46% counted as PIPED-PRIMARY and excluded - the household holds a public connection and the catchment is a supplement/backup, which is how a JMP main-source question would resolve it; splitting it 50/50 would be arbitrary and would invent 2.2 points of unpiped population. The alternative (all-catchment-primary) ceiling is recorded in bounds_notes. Borehole = individual well 0.50 (the census label does not say drilled vs dug; American Samoan household wells tap the volcanic aquifer and are drilled/driven, so Borehole is the better fit - flagged). OtherUnpiped = catchment-only 0.47 + some other source 0.64 = 1.11; the 'other' label leads with 'standpipe' (which would be piped) but is dominated by spring/river/creek, so the whole 0.64 is assigned to OtherUnpiped as the conservative choice at this magnitude. Packaged and Delivered = null: the census has no bottled or vendor/tanker category at all, so neither can be filled or zeroed. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the Census 'source of water' item is a HOUSEHOLD SUPPLY question, not a main-DRINKING-water question (rubric rule 1) - bottled water is likely a common drinking source alongside a piped household supply and is invisible here. Territory-wide table with no urban/rural split; ASM is treated as ~100% urban in most classifications, but the same values are written to both strata.
bounds_notes: If 'public system and catchment' (4.46%) were instead resolved as catchment-primary, OtherUnpiped would be 5.57 rather than 1.11 - that is the upper bound. Packaged is unbounded by this table (no bottled category).

source: ABS, Environmental Issues: Water Use and Conservation, Mar 2013 (cat. 4602.0.55.003), summarised in AIHW Australia's Health 2018; WA bore figure from ABS 4616.5.55.001 (2003)
mapping_notes: No main-drinking-source-style question exists for Australia. The only national instrument located (ABS 4602.0.55.003, discontinued after 2013) asks which sources a household USED, allowing multiple answers, so its percentages do not sum to 100 and cannot be placed in the fill columns (rubric rule 5). The section file itself concludes 'multi-source usage survey, not main drinking source - cannot cleanly derive single-source %'. The capital/non-capital split reported by ABS is also not a clean urban/rural split (non-capital includes large regional cities that are fully mains-served), so it cannot be repurposed as URBAN/RURAL even as a proxy. No category can be evidenced at ~0 either: rainwater-tank and bore reliance outside the capitals is described as real and material, and bottled/delivered water is not quantified at all. All eight fill columns therefore left null rather than fabricated.
bounds_notes: Recorded, NOT filled (all multi-response 'used as a source' figures, 2013): 93% of households (8.3M) used mains/town water; 99% in capital cities vs 84% outside capitals; rainwater tank used as a source by 19% of capital-city vs 37% of non-capital households. WA only (ABS 4616.5.55.001, 2003): ~21% of mains-connected WA households also use bore water. Implied bounds: because 'used mains' is multi-response and therefore an over-count of mains reliance, the 7% national (16% non-capital, 1% capital) who used no mains water at all is a LOWER bound on the share whose main source is self-supply; there is no corresponding upper bound, and no evidence for splitting that residual between rainwater (OtherUnpiped) and bores (Borehole).

source: EurEau, 'Europe's Water in Figures - 2026 edition', Annex Fig.1 (ref. period 2022-2024): 92% of population connected to a public drinking-water network; corroborated by BMLUK/OVGW reporting that ~7% of the population uses private wells/springs
mapping_notes: Connection-rate proxy (rubric rule 4). Residual = 100-92 = 8%; the country-specific BMLUK/OVGW statement gives ~7% on private wells/springs, so 7.0 is used rather than the raw 8% ceiling. The source does NOT split wells from springs, so the entire self-supply residual is placed in Borehole as the single best-supported category and OtherUnpiped is set to 0 to avoid double-counting - the reliable quantity is Borehole+OtherUnpiped = 7%, and an unquantified share of that is alpine spring supply that properly belongs in OtherUnpiped. Delivered = 0 (no tanker/vendor supply documented; ceiling on all non-network supply is 8%). Packaged left null: a connection rate says nothing about bottled water as main drinking source. Piped (92%) excluded from our columns per rubric.
bounds_notes: EurEau footnote p.9: 'People not connected to water supply may include households with private wells and people with no permanent fixed housing' - so 8% is an upper ceiling on household self-supply, not a measured self-supply share.

source: EurEau, 'Europe's Water in Figures - 2026 edition', Annex Fig.1 (ref. period 2022-2024): 98.9% of population connected to a public drinking-water network
mapping_notes: Connection-rate proxy (rubric rule 4). Residual = 1.1%. No Belgian source describes the residual's composition beyond EurEau's generic footnote ('may include households with private wells'), so the whole residual is placed in Borehole and OtherUnpiped/Delivered set to 0 to avoid double-counting; treat Borehole+OtherUnpiped = 1.1% as the reliable quantity. Regional utility reports (Belgaqua/AquaFlanders/Aquawal) were not accessible, so no urban/rural or source-type split exists. Packaged left null - not measured by a connection rate.
bounds_notes: 1.1% is a ceiling on all non-network household supply, and EurEau notes it also includes people with no permanent fixed housing, so the true private-well share is lower.

source: CBS Netherlands, Caribisch Nederland; waterbalans (StatLine 85799NED) and Drinkwatergebruik op Bonaire longread (2024); Dutch Water Sector on Saba's 2019 desalination/distribution scheme
mapping_notes: CBS publishes household CONNECTION COUNTS with no household denominator, so no percentage can be computed without inventing a household-size assumption: Bonaire 10,803 connections against a population of 27,611 (2024); Sint Eustatius 1,133 connections against a population of 3,348 (2024); Saba has no CBS production or connection series at all. Dividing connections by population would give a per-capita ratio, not a share of households on the network, so nothing is filled. Additional complication: BES is a single ISO code covering three separate islands with different water histories, so even a correct island figure would need population weighting before it could become a BES row.
bounds_notes: Qualitative direction only: Bonaire and Sint Eustatius are largely on piped desalinated supply; Saba historically relied on rainwater cisterns (OtherUnpiped) plus trucked water (Delivered) and only completed desalination + village piped distribution around 2019, so any pre-2019 source would misstate today's position. Saba is roughly 2,000 people, a small weight in a BES-wide figure. Follow-up: a CBS household-count denominator for Bonaire/Statia would convert the connection counts into a fillable coverage rate.

source: Annali di Igiene, 'Factors Influencing Water Consumption in the Kingdom of Bahrain and Environmental Consequences of Bottled Water Consumption' (2022), survey n=483, Apr-May 2019
mapping_notes: Nothing filled. Per rubric rule 6, the only available numbers come from a small-n (n=483) convenience-sample consumption survey, not a main-drinking-source census question, so Packaged must not be filled from them. The category structure is also incompatible: 'filtered water' 35.90% is ambiguous and most likely point-of-use filtered TAP water, which is piped, not Packaged. I also considered filling Borehole=0 (Bahrain is desalination-network supplied and its groundwater is saline) but the section provides no evidence on household well use at all, so 0 would be an assertion rather than a finding.
bounds_notes: Recorded but NOT filled: predominant water type in the 2019 survey (n=483) - filtered 35.90%, bottled 34.50%, tap 8.90%. Historical bottled/barrelled share 36.86% (2001) -> 25.75% (2011). Together these bound Packaged-as-main-source at roughly 25-35%, but from an attitudinal/consumption frame. Delivered (tanker) not separately quantified. Bahrain iGA/data.gov.bh Census 2020 housing datasets were searched and no water-source table was located - that is the follow-up.

source: Agency for Statistics of BiH (BHAS), Census 2013, Book 5 'Dwellings, Housing and Housing Conditions', Table 3.5 'Occupied dwellings by type of potable water supply system' (p.674), n=1,133,492 occupied dwellings
mapping_notes: Direct census table with 11 source categories. EXCLUDED as piped: public/community mains 65.3% and rural/local water-scheme piped 19.7% (JMP counts community/village piped schemes as piped). Borehole = own pump/hydrophore ('vlastiti hidrofor') 12.2% + drilled well 0.15% + artesian well 0.06% = 12.41 - the hydrophore category is explicitly a pressurised, pumped household system, which is the rubric's 'own drilled well with an electric pump/hydrophore'. OtherUnpiped = dug well 0.87% + regulated spring 0.32% + other 0.57% = 1.76 - I used the section file's FINER split and put the DUG well portion (0.87) in OtherUnpiped rather than in Borehole, which is where the section's own suggested mapping (Borehole ~13.4%) had put it. Packaged = bottled water from shop 0.10%. Delivered = water tank/cistern 0.10% (the master table glosses this as 'cistern truck'; if it is instead a static rainwater cistern it belongs in OtherUnpiped - 0.1pp either way). JUDGMENT CALL: street fountain 0.21% was EXCLUDED from OtherUnpiped and treated as piped, per the rubric's explicit rule that public taps/standpipes/village tap-houses count as piped; the section's suggested mapping had included it in OtherUnpiped. Sum check: 85.0 piped + 14.37 our categories = 99.37, within rounding of the census total.
bounds_notes: No urban/rural split published; municipality-level Table 3.5.1 would allow a proxy urban/rural build but was not extracted, so the national distribution is applied to both strata - this understates rural Borehole/OtherUnpiped and overstates urban. Eurostat env_wat_pop 69.7% connected (2019) is consistent with the 65.3% public-mains census figure. 2013 reference year is the most recent census. Pump-type signal: electric-pumped hydrophore wells (12.2%) vs simple dug/drilled/artesian wells (~1.1%) is roughly an 11:1 electric:manual ratio.
verification: CONFIRMED 2026-08-08 vs Census 2013 Book 5 Table 3.5 pp.674-675 (hydrofor 12.17%, wells 1.08%)

source: SAFE Saint-Barth (island water utility) crisis/supply pages; corroborated by Outremers360 — qualitative only, no household statistics
mapping_notes: The single fillable value is an evidence-based zero. Saint-Barthelemy has NO natural freshwater resource — the island depends on seawater desalination (SAFE, capacity 190 m3/hr) distributed through a network, with private cisterns as backup storage. With no freshwater aquifer there is no drilled-borehole population, so Borehole = 0 (rubric rule 3). Everything else is left null: the split between network-desalinated piped water (excluded from our columns), cistern/rainwater backup (OtherUnpiped) and bottled (Packaged) is not quantified anywhere, and INSEE does not ask a water-source question for French COMs, so there is no census route to it. Note that the cisterns here are described as BACKUP STORAGE rather than a primary source, which is a different situation from Anguilla or the BVI and is why no OtherUnpiped value is guessed.
bounds_notes: No quantified household figures exist. INSEE dossier complet COM-97701, safestbarth.fr, Outremers360, BRGM Infoterre and SISPEA were all checked; the INSEE census for French COMs carries no 'source d'eau' variable. BLM is dropped by drop_small_island_nations in the model (rubric rule 10); the row is produced for dataset completeness.

source: Government of Bermuda, 2016 Population and Housing Census Report (full-text extraction confirms NO water-supply question); Public Health (Water Storage) Regulations 1951; Dept. of Works / Watlington Waterworks via UN Stats CARICOM presentation 2019
mapping_notes: A derived_assumption row with OtherUnpiped set high was considered and REJECTED. The mandated-rooftop-catchment fact (Public Health (Water Storage) Regulations 1951, applying to virtually all buildings) establishes that nearly every Bermudian dwelling HAS a rainwater cistern, but our columns require the MAIN DRINKING source, and the two are demonstrably different things in exactly this kind of territory. The decisive evidence is regional: in Anguilla, cisterns supply 78.9% of households yet only 35.9% drink from them (60.7% drink bottled); in the BVI, private piped/cistern supplies 31.9% of households yet only 16.2% drink from unpiped sources (80.5% drink bottled). Both are cistern-mandate, catchment-culture islands with the same climate and income profile as Bermuda. Assuming Bermuda's main DRINKING source is rainwater would therefore likely be wrong by 40-60 percentage points in the same direction, and there is no Bermuda figure to pin the Packaged share to. Not filled.
bounds_notes: Qualitative context recorded for completeness: rooftop rainwater catchment legally mandated since 1951 on effectively all buildings; supplemented by ~500M imperial gallons/year from private and public wells plus desalination (Dept. of Works / Watlington Waterworks 2018). So the SUPPLY-side picture is near-100% OtherUnpiped + some Borehole + some desalinated trucked/piped water — directionally certain but uncitable at a number, and not the same as the drinking-source split we need. Regional analogues (AIA 60.7% bottled, VGB 80.5% bottled) suggest Packaged is the single largest drinking category in Bermuda too. Follow-up: Bermuda has no household water question in any census; a consumer survey or Dept. of Works customer data would be needed.

source: Barbados Statistical Service, 2010 Population and Housing Census Volume 1, Table 09.12 (n=78,936 occupied dwellings)
mapping_notes: Evidence-based zeros per rubric rule 3 — Barbados is effectively fully piped on the BWA network. Table 09.12: Piped into dwelling 94.2% + Piped into yard 2.5% + Friend/relative pipe 0.9% (= piped to neighbour, piped per rubric) + Public standpipe 0.4% (piped per rubric) = 98.0% piped, all excluded from our columns; Stream/spring/well ~0.005%; Other 0.1%; Not stated 1.8%. OtherUnpiped = 0.1 (the 'Other' 0.1% plus the 0.005% stream/spring/well, which rounds to 0.1). Borehole = 0 because no drilled-tubewell category exists and the entire combined stream/spring/well group is 0.005% — five thousandths of one percent — so any borehole component is indistinguishable from zero; per rubric the well portion of a stream/spring/well group would in any case default to OtherUnpiped. Delivered = 0: no tanker category, and a fully networked island with 98% piped leaves no room. Packaged = 0 is the weakest value in this row — see flags: the 2010 census asked about household SUPPLY, not drinking, so a bottled-drinking population is not excluded by this table; it is set to 0 rather than null because the residual after piped + not-stated is 0.1%, which caps ALL four of our categories together at ~0.1% within this question's frame. Single stratum (11 parishes, no urban/rural), values applied to both.
bounds_notes: Hard ceiling from the census: all four unpiped categories together <=~0.1% of dwellings (plus 1.8% not stated, which is the real uncertainty band). Caveat on Packaged: unlike Anguilla and the BVI, Barbados has no drinking-specific census question, so the 0 for Packaged rests on the supply question plus Barbados's well-documented high-quality limestone-aquifer tap water rather than on a direct measurement — if a Barbados drinking-source survey ever surfaces, Packaged is the value most likely to move. 2021 census (if released) not checked.

source: DEPS, 'Report of the Brunei Population and Housing Census 2021 (BPP 2021): Demographic, Household and Housing Characteristics', Nov 2022 - confirmed via GHDx to contain a household water-supply variable, but the PDF/tables were not retrieved (404 on automated fetch)
mapping_notes: No values obtained. The correct primary document has been identified and is confirmed to contain the needed variable, but no number from it appears in the research files, and the rubric forbids inventing values. Nothing filled.
bounds_notes: Follow-up: manually download the BPP 2021 'Demographic, Household and Housing Characteristics' report from deps.mofe.gov.bn or brucensus.gov.bn - it very likely contains a directly usable household water-supply table with an urban/rural split.

source: EurEau, 'Europe's Water in Figures - 2026 edition', Annex Fig.1 (ref. period 2022-2024): 99.4% connected to a public drinking-water network; SVGW commentary on private extraction (some private household wells, especially farms)
mapping_notes: Connection-rate proxy (rubric rule 4). Residual = 0.6%. SVGW describes the private-extraction remainder as mostly agricultural/commercial with some private household wells (farms), which supports Borehole rather than springs/surface, so the full residual goes to Borehole; OtherUnpiped and Delivered set to 0 to avoid double-counting. SVGW gives no household-level percentage, so the 0.6% is the EurEau residual, not an SVGW measurement. Packaged left null.
bounds_notes: 0.6% is a ceiling on all non-network household supply; SVGW's private-extraction volume is dominated by agriculture/industry, so the household share is at or below this.

source: CNSEE/ICF International, Enquete Demographique et de Sante du Congo (EDSC-II) 2011-2012, Final Report FR267 (2013), Tableau 2.1, p.16 (n=11,632 households). Fieldwork 2011-2012; survey_year set to 2011.
mapping_notes: Category-by-category (Urban/Rural %). EXCLUDED as piped: Robinet logement 5.3/0.4, Robinet cour 33.4/2.0, Robinet public 39.7/5.1 (public tap = piped per JMP) -> piped total 78.4 urban / 7.5 rural. Borehole = 'Puits a pompe/forage' only: 8.7/11.9 (rubric rule 9: forage/pump-well -> Borehole). Packaged = 'Eau en bouteille' 3.9/0.2. OtherUnpiped = Puits creuse protege 3.0/7.3 + Source protegee 1.7/8.5 + Eau de pluie 0.0/5.8 + Puits creuse non protege 1.8/11.1 + Source non protegee 1.0/21.9 + Eau de surface 0.0/22.0 + Autre 1.5/3.6 = 9.0 urban / 80.2 rural. Delivered = null: the EDSC-II table has NO camion-citerne/charrette line item, so tanker/cart users are unidentifiable (they would sit inside 'Autre', 1.5/3.6, which I assigned to OtherUnpiped); a 0 would not be evidence-supported. DEVIATION from the section file's 'Suggested mapping', which lumped protected+unprotected dug wells ('Puits creuse') into Borehole for a 19.7% total: rubric rule 9 explicitly sends dug wells to OtherUnpiped, so only 'Puits a pompe/forage' is counted as Borehole here. Sum check: urban 78.4+3.9+8.7+9.0 = 100.0; rural 7.5+0.2+11.9+80.2 = 99.8 (rounding). Households, not population; DHS asks main household drinking-water source.
bounds_notes: Delivered is bounded above by 'Autre' (1.5% urban / 3.6% rural). If dug wells were counted as Borehole (the section file's suggestion), Borehole would be 13.5 urban / 30.3 rural and OtherUnpiped 4.2 / 61.8.
verification: CONFIRMED 2026-08-08 vs DHS FR267 Tableau 2.1 p.16 (all figures exact)

source: curacao.nu, 'Curacao heeft genoeg drinkwater, maar niet voor iedereen' (2024/2025) — journalistic reporting of Aqualectra connection counts
mapping_notes: Only a connection proxy exists and it is journalistic rather than statistical: ~1,100 households (~2%) have no Aqualectra connection at all, plus a further ~2% disconnected for non-payment, i.e. ~96% actively connected. The article describes purchased-water cisterns/barrels and rainwater for the unconnected but gives no island-wide percentage, so the ~4% residual cannot be split between Delivered and OtherUnpiped. Rubric rule 4 caps proxy-derived values at 'med' confidence and requires the source itself to name the residual's composition — it does not. CBS Curacao 2011 and 2023 census publications were PDF-searched and contain zero water-source tables.
bounds_notes: Ceiling: <=4% of households off the public network (2024), plausibly splitting between OtherUnpiped (rainwater/cisterns) and Delivered (purchased/trucked water into cisterns and barrels) — proportions unknown. Public supply is desalinated but network-distributed = piped, excluded from our columns.

source: Czech Statistical Office (CSU), press release 170381-22, 25 Nov 2022, Census 2021 (ref. 26 Mar 2021) - occupied HOUSES by water supply
mapping_notes: Section reports only occupied HOUSES: 82.0% public mains only, >10% private source only (well), 6.8% both. A population/dwelling-level figure is required, so I derived a conservative national estimate: the section states flats are ~50% of dwellings and are ~100% on the public network, so national well-only share ~= 0.50 x 10% = 5.0%. Private household sources in Czechia ('vlastni studna', typically pumped) mapped to Borehole per rubric (own drilled/pumped well). The 6.8% dual-supply houses were EXCLUDED entirely (they have a mains connection, so mains is the more likely main drinking source) - including half of them would raise the estimate to ~6.7%, and including all of them ~8.4%. No urban/rural split exists in the source; houses skew rural and flats urban, so 5.0 applied to both strata overstates urban and understates rural. Note also that the 10% is a dwelling share, and house households are larger than flat households, so the person-weighted share is somewhat higher than 5.0 - the fill is deliberately conservative.
bounds_notes: Plausible national Borehole range 5.0-8.4 depending on treatment of the 6.8% dual-supply houses. Regional public-mains share ranges 71.2% (Plzensky) to 95.7% (Prague), implying rural/peripheral Borehole shares materially above 5% and Prague well below it.

source: Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), 'Anschlussgrad sowie Wasserabgabe an Haushalte', 2022 data: 99.5% connected to public water supply (82,788,000 of 83,237,000 people)
mapping_notes: Connection-rate proxy (rubric rule 4). Residual = 0.5% (~449,000 people). Placed entirely in Borehole (private wells) with OtherUnpiped/Delivered = 0 to avoid double-counting; treat Borehole+OtherUnpiped = 0.5% as the reliable quantity. Umweltbundesamt small-scale supplies (<1,000 households) serving ~12% of the connected population are part of the PUBLIC system and are therefore piped - explicitly NOT counted here. Confidence capped at med per rubric rule 4 even though the Destatis connection rate itself is high confidence. Packaged left null.
bounds_notes: No urban/rural split in Destatis. An older Wikipedia table citing JMP/WHO-Europe 2006 shows 100% urban / 97% rural house connections - historical, weak, not used to differentiate the strata.

source: University of Copenhagen press release on the Schullehner/Hansen (GEUS) nationwide study, Nov 2023: >95% of Danes supplied by ~2,600 public waterworks; ~4% (~237,000 people) supplied by private boreholes from ~50,000 registered private wells
mapping_notes: The strongest fill in this batch because the source names BOREHOLES specifically rather than an undifferentiated 'private supply' residual - so no residual_allocation_uncertain flag is needed and 4.0 goes cleanly into Borehole. OtherUnpiped and Delivered = 0 (the >95% public + 4% borehole accounting leaves ~1% unexplained, well within rounding). Population basis, not household basis. National figure applied to both strata per rubric rule 2 - in reality private boreholes are rural-concentrated, so the urban value overstates and the rural understates.
bounds_notes: ~50,000 registered private wells, each serving fewer than 9 households. Primary GEUS dataset page was not located; the figure comes from several 2023 articles reporting the same study.

source: National Statistics Office / Ministry of Health, Eritrea Population and Health Survey (EPHS) 2010, Table 2-12, p.33 (n=10,588 households). WHO-AFRO hosted.
mapping_notes: Used the 'Total urban' and 'Rural' columns (the table also splits urban into Asmara / Other Town; Asmara-only and Other-Town-only values are in bounds_notes). EXCLUDED as piped: Piped residence/yard 38.7/0.3 + Public tap 17.9/35.6 + Private tap 11.6/0.3 = 68.2 urban / 36.2 rural. Packaged = Bottled water 2.5/0.1. Delivered = Tanker Truck 25.6/3.8 (note EPHS itself classifies trucked water as non-improved, unlike JMP, but the JMP category assignment here is 'Delivered' regardless). Borehole = 'Protected public well' 1.6/13.3; OtherUnpiped = 'Unprotected public well' 0.9/22.3 + 'Surface water' 0.4/23.3 = 1.3 / 45.6. JUDGMENT CALL on the two well rows: EPHS says only 'protected'/'unprotected public well' and never distinguishes dug well from tubewell/borehole. I split them - protected public wells in Eritrea are overwhelmingly handpump-equipped drilled/lined wells (protection in practice means a sealed headworks + pump), whereas unprotected public wells are open hand-dug wells - so protected -> Borehole and unprotected -> OtherUnpiped. This is the single largest interpretive step in the row; confidence downgraded to med for the Borehole/OtherUnpiped split (Packaged and Delivered remain high-confidence). source: Foster, T. & Gonzalez, D. (2022), Self-supply of water in Asia and the Pacific: FSM Country Profile, UTS-ISF / Water for Women / UNICEF, citing the FSM 2010 Census main drinking-water source table

Mapping: Packaged = 8 (bottled). Piped and EXCLUDED = public utility 14 + community system 17 = 31; community/village reticulated systems and their tap-houses count as piped per the rubric. OtherUnpiped = 43 (rainwater tank) + 9 (protected 7 + unprotected 2 wells) + 7 (spring/river/lake) + 2 (other) = 61. Borehole = 0. This DEVIATES from the report's own suggested mapping, which put the 9% of wells into Borehole: (a) the census instrument has no tubewell/borehole category at all - its categories are 'protected well' and 'unprotected well', which in JMP terms are the dug-well rows, not the 'Tubewell, borehole' row; (b) the section's pump-type note states FSM outer islands use 'shallow, hand-dug wells' alongside rain catchments, with many hand-drawn rather than pump-equipped. Both point to dug rather than drilled wells, which the rubric assigns to OtherUnpiped. Delivered = 0: the census offers no tanker/cart/vendor category and none is described in the section; any delivered water would sit inside the unspecified 'other' 2%, which was assigned to OtherUnpiped. National figure applied to both URBAN and RURAL per rubric rule 2; the source reports state-level self-supply instead (Chuuk 69%, Kosrae 59%, Yap 46%, Pohnpei 10%), and since Pohnpei holds the main urban centres this implies real urban self-supply is well below 61 and rural well above it - the row is a national average, not a true stratum split. | VERIFIER: national figures rest on UTS analysis of census microdata (non-official); Yap 46.2% and Pohnpei 10.0% verified exactly against state Table H03; Chuuk table unpublished.
bounds_notes: State-level self-supply spread (Chuuk 69%, Kosrae 59%, Yap 46%, Pohnpei 10%) is the best available proxy for how far the national 61% would move under a genuine urban/rural split, but the source gives no urban/rural denominators so no split was attempted. Sum check: 8 (Packaged) + 0 (Delivered) + 0 (Borehole) + 61 (OtherUnpiped) + 31 (piped utility+community) = 100.0, no overshoot. source: DWQR, 'Private Water Supplies - Drinking Water Quality in Scotland 2023' (3.5% of population; regulated tier 5,160 supplies / 124,846 people: spring 2,124, watercourse 1,119, borehole 1,003, well 377, loch/rainwater/mixed 200); DWI 'Drinking Water 2023 - Private water supplies in England' (1.47%, 849,800 people); DWI Wales 2023 (2%, 64,187 people; surface-water-influenced 37.04%, groundwater 31.73%, unknown 31.05%, mains 0.18%); DAERA/NI DWI Feb 2026 (<1%)
mapping_notes: This is the only country in the batch where the regulator publishes a source MIX for private supplies, so the residual could be split rather than dumped into one category. Two-step derivation: (1) UK population share on private supply = ~1.7% (section's population-weighted 1.6-1.8% midpoint of England 1.47%, Wales 2%, Scotland 3.5%, NI <1%). (2) Scotland's regulated-tier source counts give borehole 1,003 / 4,823 = 20.8% and everything else = 79.2% (spring 44.0%, watercourse 23.2%, well 7.8%, loch/rainwater/mixed 4.1%). Per rubric, 'borehole' -> Borehole; dug/traditional 'well', springs, watercourses, lochs and rainwater all -> OtherUnpiped. So Borehole = 1.7 x 0.208 = 0.35 -> 0.4 and OtherUnpiped = 1.7 x 0.792 = 1.35 -> 1.3. Wales corroborates the shape (groundwater 31.7% vs surface-influenced 37% + unknown 31%) but does not separate boreholes from wells, so Scotland's mix was used. KEY CAVEAT: the Scottish mix is a count of SUPPLIES, not of population, and is applied UK-wide. Delivered = 0. Packaged null. National figures applied to both strata per rubric rule 2 - private supplies are overwhelmingly rural, so the urban values materially overstate and the rural values materially understate; local-authority detail exists for Wales and Scotland (e.g. Highland 32,595 people on regulated PWS) if a proper urban/rural weighting is wanted later.
bounds_notes: Constituent-country private-supply shares: England 1.47%, Wales 2%, Scotland 3.5%, NI <1%. Scotland's unregulated (Type B) tier is not included in the source-mix counts used. England and NI figures were search-summarised rather than read from the primary PDF; Wales and Scotland were verified directly.

source: SISPEA (services.eaufrance.fr), 'Departement Guadeloupe (971), 2023'; Coalition Eau aggregator
mapping_notes: Evidence-based zeros for the three measurable categories. SISPEA 2023 covers 388,727 inhabitants across 13 public water services with compliance of 98.4% / 97.8%; the territory is fully networked, and the documented deficit is INTERMITTENT SUPPLY (daily cuts, 'tours d'eau', 60%+ network losses, ~400,000 people affected by chronic outages per Coalition Eau) rather than a population on alternative sources. That distinction is the substantive finding for this row and matters for CIL framing: Guadeloupe's vulnerability is a connected-but-failing network, not self-supply, so it should NOT appear in the model as unpiped population. Packaged left null: bottled consumption is very likely elevated by the outages, but no main-drinking-source figure exists and rubric rule 6 forbids filling Packaged from behavioural inference. Single stratum, applied to both URBAN and RURAL.
bounds_notes: JMP SDG estimate cited for context: 95.7% safely managed — that is a network/service-level indicator, not a source-type split, and is not used. During rationing episodes the utility distributes water by tanker; that is emergency supplementation, not a main source, which is why Delivered is 0 rather than a positive value. The confidence is low because the zeros are INFERRED from full network coverage rather than measured by any household question — INSEE's Guadeloupe housing dossier carries no water-source variable.

source: Central Statistical Office of Grenada, 'Water Supply by Parish, 2011' (Population & Housing Census 2011), cross-verified against Census Report 2011 p.173 (n=36,111 households)
mapping_notes: National 2011 categories: Public piped into dwelling 73.5% + Public piped into yard 5.2% + Public standpipe 6.6% = 85.3% piped (standpipes are piped per rubric), all excluded. Delivered = Truck borne 0.1%. OtherUnpiped = 14.6% = Private piped into dwelling 4.9 + Private catchment not piped 3.6 + Spring/River 2.5 + Other 3.6. Two judgment calls are embedded here. (1) 'Private piped into dwelling' is treated as private rainwater catchment piped in, NOT as network piped: the census's own Carriacou row proves it, because Carriacou has no NAWASA network at all yet reports 49.9% private piped alongside 44.3% private catchment not piped — the private-piped category on Carriacou can only be cistern water. Carriacou is roughly 6% of Grenadian households, so ~3.0 of the national 4.9pp is Carriacou cistern water. (2) 'Other' 3.6% is included in OtherUnpiped as the JMP-style residual bucket, since the piped options are all separately enumerated and 'Other' therefore cannot be network water. Borehole is null: boreholes are not separately captured and would sit inside 'Other', so filling Borehole would double-count against OtherUnpiped (rubric rule 7). Packaged null — not asked in this table. Single stratum (by parish only), applied to both URBAN and RURAL. Sum check: 85.3 piped + 14.6 + 0.1 = 100.0, exact.
bounds_notes: Alternative OtherUnpiped constructions if the two judgment calls are reversed: 11.0% (excluding 'Other'), 9.7% (the section file's own suggested mapping = catchment + spring/river + other, treating private piped as piped), or 6.1% (excluding both 'Other' and private piped). The 14.6% figure used here is the most inclusive defensible reading. Sub-territory variation is large and is the strongest signal in this row: Carriacou, with no NAWASA access, is 49.9% private piped + 44.3% private catchment not piped, i.e. ~94% cistern-based, against a near-fully-networked main island — if Carriacou is ever modelled separately it should not inherit the national value.

source: Berner et al., 'Domestic water supply in rural Greenland - sufficiency, affordability and accessibility', Int. J. Circumpolar Health, 2022 (StatBank Greenland + Nukissiorfiit meter records)
mapping_notes: DELIBERATELY not filled, and this is the most consequential judgement call in the batch. The headline finding is that in settlements under 500 inhabitants, 20% of households are piped and 80% are un-piped - but the study says those 80% collect treated water from public TAPHOUSES (average 90m from home). The rubric is explicit that public taps/standpipes/village tap-houses count as PIPED in JMP terms and must not enter our columns, so the section's suggested mapping of 'OtherUnpiped ~ 80%' would be wrong here. The only part that genuinely belongs in OtherUnpiped is the untreated natural water (river/lake/iceberg ice) used alongside taphouse water, and the study does not quantify what share of households rely on it as their MAIN drinking source. Two further blockers: the 80% covers only settlements <500 inhabitants, not all rural population, and no national or town-level piped share was retrieved, so the figure cannot be population-weighted (regional piped-home share ranges 1-65% by municipality). Filling anything would either double-count piped taphouse users as unpiped or extrapolate a sub-population to the nation.
bounds_notes: Rural settlements (<500 inhabitants): 20% of households piped, 80% un-piped and collecting from public taphouses ~90m away plus untreated natural water; regional piped-home share 1-65% by municipality. Most Greenlanders live in piped towns, so the national unpiped share is materially lower than 80%. Recorded as bounds only - do NOT treat 80% as national or as OtherUnpiped.

source: ARS Guyane, 'Etat des lieux en sante environnement', Rapport CA1200000/1036545, 21/12/2023, section 13.1 pp.69-70
mapping_notes: Not filled, despite a solid headline number, because the residual demonstrably contains piped-category users. ARS reports ~15% of the population (~30,000 inhabitants) without drinking-water access via the public network (2018/2014-based, described as stable). But the source's own list of what those people use includes 'bornes fontaines monetiques' (31 monetised standpipes) — and standpipes count as PIPED per the rubric — alongside forages with HCl treatment (~10 devices, -> Borehole), 36 pompes a motricite humaine (handpumps, -> Borehole), and eaux de pluie / puits / eau du fleuve (-> OtherUnpiped). No numeric split is given for any of these. So 15% is not even a clean ceiling on our four columns, and allocating it to OtherUnpiped under rubric rule 4 would both overstate the unpiped share and mis-assign a real borehole population. Left null pending a proper split. Note also that the 15% is a share of POPULATION, not households, which matters in a territory with very large household sizes in the interior.
bounds_notes: SOURCE QUALITY IS HIGH even though nothing is filled — the limitation is the questionnaire/definition, not the data. Ceiling: <=15% of population (~30,000 people) off the public network, but this includes standpipe (borne fontaine) users who are piped per JMP. Fondation pour le Logement (Feb 2023) counts 18,000 informal dwellings unconnected. Qualitative geography: 'bourgs reconnus', 'bourgs spontanes', 'hameaux fleuves' and 'sites isoles' behave very differently and would need separate treatment. PHASE-2 SIGNAL: French Guiana is one of the very few places in this entire exercise with a hard handpump count — 36 pompes a motricite humaine, plus ~10 treated forages — making it a rare documented CIL-resilient borehole population in a high-income jurisdiction. Follow-up: Office de l'Eau Guyane 2021 / HCSP 2021 may carry the per-source population counts behind the ARS table.

source: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census of Population and Housing (Island Areas), table HBG52 'Source of Water', DECENNIALGU2010, geography 0400000US66 (n=50,567 occupied housing units). Counts pulled directly from the Census API 2026-08-07.
mapping_notes: Full table: public system only 49,658 = 98.20%; public system and catchment 584 = 1.15%; individual well 41 = 0.08%; catchment/tanks/drums only 147 = 0.29%; some other source 137 = 0.27%. Sums to 99.99 (rounding). EXCLUDED as piped: public-only 98.20 + hybrid public+catchment 1.15 (same piped-primary decision as ASM/MNP - the household has a public connection, catchment is supplementary) = 99.35. bounds_notes: OtherUnpiped ceiling 1.71 if the public+catchment hybrid were resolved as catchment-primary.

source: Eurostat env_wat_pop (population connected to public water supply), cross-checked against DZS Census 2021 dwellings file

source: Statistical Centre of Iran census series / JMP-cited historical estimates (1996/2006/2011) as summarised in 'Water supply and sanitation in Iran'
mapping_notes: The section supports NO direct source-type percentages - only improved/unimproved aggregates: urban improved 98% (2011); rural improved 90%, of which 87pp are house connections. I filled OtherUnpiped from the UNIMPROVED complement only: urban 100-98 = 2.0, rural 100-90 = 10.0. This is defensible under JMP definitions because 'unimproved' by construction excludes boreholes and protected wells/springs (those are improved) and consists of unprotected dug wells, unprotected springs and surface water - all of which map to OtherUnpiped. Borehole left NULL, not zero: Iran has ~500,000 wells (mostly motorised) but the improved 98%/90% aggregates do not break out what share of households use a borehole as their main source, so there is no basis for a number. Qanats/karez (~60,000 still in use, gravity-fed, non-electric) are a spring analogue and would belong in OtherUnpiped, but the ones feeding village networks are piped and are inside the 'improved' 87pp house-connection figure. The rural 3pp gap (90% improved minus 87pp house connections) is improved-but-not-piped-into-dwelling - public taps, protected wells or protected springs - and could not be split, so it is unallocated.
bounds_notes: CEILING interpretation: the unimproved residual may also contain tanker/vendor water (Delivered), which the section reports is used in water-stressed provinces (Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan) without any national percentage - so 2.0/10.0 are ceilings for OtherUnpiped, not clean measurements. Reference year 2011 is stale; the 2016 SCI census and MIDHS 2010 very likely carry a proper source-type table (amar.org.ir not fetched, MIDHS percentages not extracted). Context not usable as fills: ~500,000 wells nationally (many unlicensed), ~60,000 qanats, ~27,000 villages / 10M+ residents reported facing water shortages.

source: Jersey Water, 'About Us' (mains supplies >90% of the population); corroborating gov.je-sourced statement that the remaining 10% is supplied from private abstractions predominantly from boreholes and wells
mapping_notes: Population basis preferred (~10%) over the property basis (~2,800 properties, ~5% of households, per BBC) because our schema is a share of population. The source says 'predominantly boreholes and wells' without splitting them, so the full 10% goes to Borehole with OtherUnpiped/Delivered = 0 to avoid double-counting - the reliable quantity is Borehole+OtherUnpiped = 10%, and the 'wells' portion would properly sit in OtherUnpiped. Borehole is nonetheless the better-supported category here because the wording leads with boreholes. Reference year is unstated by both sources, hence survey_year null.
bounds_notes: Property-basis alternative: ~2,800 properties (~5% of households) lack a mains connection (BBC, https://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/articles/cwyn8d8exn8o). The 5% vs 10% gap is the household-vs-population basis difference.

source: MLIT/MHLW 'Basic Waterworks Statistics' (水道の基本統計), FY2021-2022; national waterworks penetration rate 97.9%
mapping_notes: Connection-rate proxy: the waterworks penetration rate (main + simple + dedicated waterworks population / total population) is 97.9%, leaving a 2.1% residual. MLIT does not itemise the residual; the section infers it is private wells (自家用井戸) in rural/mountainous areas, and Japanese household wells are essentially all drilled and electrically pumped, so I allocated it to Borehole. Per rubric rule 2, the national figure is applied to both strata because MLIT publishes only prefecture-level (not urban/rural) rates. This is directionally wrong within strata: the residual is believed to be concentrated in rural and mountainous municipalities, so URBANBorehole 2.1 is almost certainly an overstatement and RURALBorehole 2.1 an understatement. Packaged/Delivered left null - no main-drinking-source data found (Japan has non-trivial bottled and home-delivery water use that is not captured anywhere in the section).
bounds_notes: 2.1% is a CEILING on all non-waterworks supply combined, not a measured private-well share. Note 'simple waterworks' (簡易水道) and 'dedicated waterworks' are already inside the 97.9% and are piped systems, so they are correctly excluded from our columns. Prefecture-level penetration rates exist at MLIT and would allow a better urban/rural build; e-Stat Housing and Land Survey may carry a household water-source variable.

source: Department of Statistics Saint Kitts and Nevis, 'Number of Household Water Supply by Type and Parish, 2011' (2011 census, n=16,926)
mapping_notes: 2011 categories: Public piped into dwelling 90.1% + into yard 4.8% + standpipe 2.4% = 97.3% piped (excluded), leaving a single undifferentiated 'Other/Not stated' bucket of 2.7%. Under rubric rule 4 an unsplit residual may be allocated to the best-supported category with a flag, and the section file's reading is that this residual is private cisterns/wells — so OtherUnpiped = 2.7. This is deliberately flagged low confidence and should be read as a CEILING, not a measurement, for two reasons: the bucket merges genuine 'Other' with item non-response, and the census asked about household supply rather than drinking, so a bottled-drinking population (large in neighbouring AIA and VGB) is entirely invisible here. Borehole, Delivered and Packaged left null because the residual cannot be split and filling any of them would double-count against the 2.7. Parish detail: St Kitts 90.2/4.7/2.8/2.3, Nevis 89.6/5.3/1.1/4.0 — Nevis has the larger residual (4.0%). Single stratum, applied to both URBAN and RURAL.
bounds_notes: All four unpiped categories together <=2.7% nationally (<=2.3% St Kitts, <=4.0% Nevis), and that ceiling includes non-response. The 2021/22 census report (https://statistics.caricom.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/SKN-Census-Report-2021-2022.pdf, checked via pdftotext) contains NO water table at all, so 2011 remains the latest usable reference and there is no path to a refresh from the census route.

source: Kim et al., 'Water Policy of Korea for Supplying Safe Groundwater in Rural Areas', Water 2017, 9(7), 508, citing Ministry of Environment / NIER data (~2012-2015)
mapping_notes: 96.1% of the population is served by municipal waterworks (~2015); 3.9% (~2.14M people) living in rural myeon/villages drink groundwater from old, unregistered WELLS outside the municipal system. Mapped to Borehole rather than OtherUnpiped: the source describes them as groundwater wells outside the registry, and the section's pump-type note says rural Korean wells/small facilities are typically electrically pumped - not hand-dug/hand-drawn. URBANBorehole set to 0 (not null) per rubric rule 3: the source attributes the entire non-municipal share to rural myeon areas, so urban self-supply is ~0. IMPORTANT SCALE CAVEAT: 3.9% is a share of the NATIONAL population that happens to live rurally, not a share of the rural population. Expressed properly as a percent of rural population it would be several times larger (Korea's rural population share is well under 20%), but no rural-population denominator appears in the sources, so I did not derive one - RURALBorehole 3.9 should be read as a FLOOR. EXCLUDED as piped: 'village waterworks' (마을상수도, 100-2,500 users, 2.0% in 2012) and 'small-scale water supply facilities' (소규모급수시설, <100 users, 1.0%) - both are small PIPED distribution systems, which JMP counts as piped even though they are groundwater-sourced. These two also risk overlapping with the 3.9% figure, so combining them would double-count.
bounds_notes: Total non-municipal-mains population is 4-7% depending on whether the 2% village-waterworks and 1% small-facility populations are counted separately from the 3.9% unregistered-well population; the sources do not clarify the overlap. Groundwater-sourced but piped small systems are the reason the model's 'piped' share may be more grid-dependent than it looks. Reference years mix 2012 and 2015.

source: 'Water And Other Drinks Consumption Evaluation In Kuwait', n=2,500 across six governorates; supplementary J. Engineering Research (2015) tap-vs-bottled study
mapping_notes: Nothing filled. Per rubric rule 6 the available numbers are behavioural/attitudinal ('do you drink tap water'), not a main-source question, and per rubric rule 5 they are multi-response (56.29% report using BOTH tap and bottled), so they cannot be placed in mutually exclusive fill columns. I also declined to write Borehole=0: the section's '~92% of domestic/industrial fresh water is desalinated (piped)' is a supply-VOLUME share, not a household main-source measurement, and volume shares cannot be converted into population shares.
bounds_notes: Recorded but NOT filled: 20.2% report never drinking tap water at all; 56.29% use both tap and bottled; >87% use household filtration; desalination is ~92% of domestic/industrial fresh water (piped). Packaged-as-main-source is bounded below by ~20% (the pure non-tap drinkers) and above by ~76% (20.2 + 56.29 mixed users). Population is essentially fully urban, so any eventual fill can be applied to both strata. Follow-up: Central Statistical Bureau Kuwait census housing tables.

source: historisches-lexikon.li, 'Wasserversorgung' (data point dated 2005); Statistikportal Liechtenstein, 'Liechtenstein in Zahlen 2026'
mapping_notes: Not fillable. The only quantity available is volumetric and 20 years old: 2005 public waterworks delivered 6.4M m3 vs 'Selbstversorger' 1.3M m3 (~17% of volume), which mixes industrial/agricultural with household self-supply and cannot be converted to a share of population whose MAIN DRINKING source is self-supplied. The 2023 figure (49.7% groundwater / 50.3% springs) is the raw-water origin of the PUBLIC network, not household connection status, and must not be read as a household borehole/spring split.
bounds_notes: 17% self-supply by volume (2005) is a rough upper bound on household self-supply only; no population-based statistic exists.

source: Macao Water Supply Company operational data via Macao Magazine and the Wikipedia 'Water supply and sanitation in Macau' summary - near-universal piped coverage of >680,000 residents via a 754 km network; ~96% of raw water imported from Zhuhai, ~4% from local rainwater-catchment reservoirs
mapping_notes: No census/household water-source table exists (DSEC by-census table not located), so this is an inference-based row. Borehole, OtherUnpiped and Delivered set to 0 (rubric rule 3 - zeros with evidence): Macao is a fully built-up, entirely urban territory with a 754 km reticulated network reaching essentially every resident, and private wells / rainwater harvesting / tanker delivery to households have no meaningful role. Note the ~4% rainwater-catchment figure is a RAW-WATER SOURCE MIX for the utility's reservoirs, NOT household rainwater harvesting - it is distributed through the network and therefore counts as piped, not OtherUnpiped. Packaged deliberately left NULL rather than 0: no data was found on bottled water as the main drinking source, and in the Macao/Hong Kong region bottled and dispenser water as a primary drinking source is plausibly non-trivial (tap water is widely boiled or avoided), so asserting 0 would be unsupported. There is no meaningful rural population; national values are written into both strata.
bounds_notes: No household-level source anywhere; all four values rest on utility-coverage inference rather than a survey question. The Packaged share is entirely unbounded by any evidence found.

source: AFD project page, 'Renforcement de capacites de l'EEASM, a Saint-Martin' (2023–2024 context; reference year not stated in the source)
mapping_notes: Connection proxy: 89% of households connected to the public utility EEASM; the source states the remaining ~11% rely on rainwater harvesting, private desalination, or water purchased from the Dutch side, but gives no sub-split. Under rubric rule 4 the residual is allocated to the best-supported single category — OtherUnpiped, which covers rainwater harvesting and is the best available home for household-scale private desalination (not a network, so not piped, and not any of our other three) — with residual_allocation_uncertain flagged. Delivered is left null even though 'purchased from the Dutch side' is plainly a Delivered component: it is unquantified, and filling it separately would double-count against the 11.0. Borehole null: no freshwater aquifer is documented on the island. Packaged null: not addressed by the source. Utility network water on Saint-Martin is desalinated but network-distributed, so it is piped and excluded. Single stratum, applied to both URBAN and RURAL. Confidence held at low: single source, no stated reference year (2023 used as the AFD project-context year), and a connection rate is not a drinking-source measurement.
bounds_notes: All four unpiped categories together <=11% of households. Useful same-island cross-check: the Dutch side (SXM) 2011 census gives piped 83.5%, bottled 7.8%, cistern-or-well 7.4%, truck 0.5% — i.e. on Sint Maarten the non-network population splits roughly half bottled / half cistern-well, which if it carried across the border would put MAF's OtherUnpiped nearer 5-6% and Packaged nearer 5%. That analogue is recorded, not applied. Cour des Comptes 'Cahier territorial n.11' was not accessible and might carry a better figure. MAF is dropped by drop_small_island_nations in the model (rubric rule 10); the row is produced for dataset completeness.

source: IMSEE / Gouvernement de Monaco, 'Monaco en chiffres - Edition 2025', section 1.4.3: 11,045 water subscriptions for an official population of 38,423 (2024), all supplied by the sole legal utility (SMEAUX/SMEG)
mapping_notes: Evidence-based zeros (rubric rule 3). Monaco is a 100% urban microstate served by a single legal water utility with no competing private-well household supply; Borehole = 0. Delivered/OtherUnpiped/Packaged = 0 following the section's 'presumed negligible given monopoly network' - these are inferences from the monopoly structure, not measured statistics, hence tier = derived_assumption and confidence med. The 6 local sources feeding 20-50% of network volume are upstream raw-water sourcing, not household bypass, and are piped. Rural columns carry the same zeros although Monaco has no rural population.
bounds_notes: No explicit '% connected' statistic exists for Monaco; the 11,045 subscriptions figure is a household/premises count, not a coverage rate.

source: EurEau 2026 Annex (Fig.1, Fig.15) 100% connected; Water Services Corporation 'Water Production' (~66% desalination / ~34% groundwater, 134 public boreholes); Energy & Water Agency Malta, 'Green Paper on the Regulation of Groundwater Abstraction in the Maltese Islands', 2023
mapping_notes: Evidence-based zeros (rubric rule 3), and the clearest case in this batch of a real 0 rather than a blank. The 8,500+ private (largely unlicensed) boreholes are overwhelmingly agricultural/non-potable per the Green Paper and MaltaToday, so Borehole for DRINKING = 0 - do not confuse the borehole count with drinking reliance. The 134 PUBLIC boreholes feed the WSC network, so their output is piped, not Borehole. Desalinated water distributed through the network is piped per rubric. Packaged left NULL (judgement call): the section says no fill is needed because the network covers ~100% of drinking supply, but no bottled-water main-source statistic exists for Malta, so 'unknown' is more honest than 0 - same treatment as Spain.
bounds_notes: 8,500+ private boreholes; combined public+private abstraction toward ~35 million m3/year. This is an abstraction/count statistic, not a household drinking-source share.

source: US Census Bureau, 2010 Census of Population and Housing (Island Areas), table HBG52 'Source of Water', DECENNIALMP2010, geography 0400000US69 (n=20,850 occupied housing units). Note: in the CNMI dataset HBG51 is Air Conditioning and Source of Water is HBG52 - labels verified via variables.json. Counts pulled directly from the Census API 2026-08-07.
mapping_notes: Full table: public system only 16,405 = 78.68%; public system and catchment 4,006 = 19.21%; individual well 220 = 1.06%; catchment/tanks/drums only 162 = 0.78%; some other source 57 = 0.27%. Sums to 100.00. EXCLUDED as piped: public-only 78.68 + hybrid 19.21 = 97.89. HYBRID DECISION (largest in this batch): the 19.21% 'public system and catchment' is counted piped-primary for consistency with ASM/GUM, but the caveat matters more here - CNMI's public supply was historically intermittent/non-potable in places, so a real main-drinking-source question would very likely move a substantial slice of that 19.21% into OtherUnpiped (or into bottled). This is a bounded, explicitly-flagged choice, not a confident one; the ceiling is in bounds_notes. Borehole = individual well 1.06 (highest well share of the four US island areas; well type unlabelled - flagged). OtherUnpiped = catchment-only 0.78 + some other source 0.27 = 1.05. Packaged/Delivered null - no bottled or vendor category. Household supply question, not drinking-specific. Territory-wide, no urban/rural split; values written to both strata.
bounds_notes: OtherUnpiped ceiling 20.26 if the 19.21% public+catchment hybrid were resolved as catchment-primary - by far the widest hybrid uncertainty in this batch, and the reason MNP confidence is med rather than high despite exact census counts.

source: Statistics Department Montserrat, 'Household access to basic necessities, 1991–2023' (census 1991/2001/2011/2023, LFS 2018)
mapping_notes: The only published number is 'water piped into dwelling' as a share of households: 99.4% in 2023 (time series 73.3% 1991 -> 85.0% 2001 -> 95.7% 2011 -> 98.1% 2018 -> 99.4% 2023). The 0.6% residual is not itemised and, note, includes households on a yard tap or standpipe as well as any genuinely unpiped households, so 0.6% is a ceiling on ALL non-dwelling-piped arrangements, not just ours. It is assigned to OtherUnpiped (rainwater cisterns are the historical Montserrat alternative) with Borehole and Delivered set to 0 — a stated assumption rather than a measurement, but the whole residual is 0.6pp so no allocation within it can move a model result. Packaged left null: this is a supply measure, not a drinking-source question, and bottled drinking is unmeasured. Post-volcano Montserrat is ~4,400 people served by the MUL network in the northern safe zone; single stratum, applied to both URBAN and RURAL.
bounds_notes: All four unpiped categories together <=0.6% of households (2023). Follow-up option identified in the section file: the CEPAL/REDATAM 2011 census tool would allow custom cross-tabs and could produce a genuine source-type breakdown for 2011 if the residual ever matters.

source: SISPEA (services.eaufrance.fr), 'Departement Martinique (972), 2023'
mapping_notes: Same treatment as Guadeloupe. SISPEA 2023: 365,734 inhabitants across 11 services, non-conformity 3.3% microbiological / 0.1% physico-chemical; ~98.8% safely managed cited. Fully networked with no measured population on alternative sources, so Borehole, OtherUnpiped and Delivered are evidence-based zeros (rubric rule 3). Documented problems are chlordecone contamination of raw water and 'tours d'eau' rationing — again a connected-but-compromised network, not self-supply. Packaged left null: chlordecone is a strong a priori reason to expect elevated bottled drinking, and this is exactly the case rubric rule 6 covers — no main-drinking-source percentage was retrieved (the Kannari study search failed), so Packaged must not be filled from the contamination narrative. Single stratum, applied to both URBAN and RURAL.
bounds_notes: Packaged is the known gap and is likely materially non-zero: chlordecone contamination has driven documented distrust of tap water in Martinique. The Kannari dietary/exposure study is the most likely source of a real bottled-water share and was not retrievable this session — this is the single highest-value follow-up for MTQ. INSEE 'Le logement en Martinique' (2017) carries no water-source variable.

source: INSEE, 'Des conditions de logement toujours precaires a Mayotte, malgre quelques ameliorations', Insee Analyses Mayotte No. 42, 2026 (fieldwork Sept 2023 – July 2024)
mapping_notes: ARITHMETIC IS EXPLICIT because INSEE's sub-percentages are shares OF THE 25% WITHOUT RUNNING WATER, not of all households. Base: 25% of households lack running water in the dwelling (down from 28% in 2013). Within that 25%: public standpipe / borne-fontaine 51%, in-home storage 18%, well/cistern (puits/citerne) 7%, river/bottled/other 5%, supply from neighbours/family 4%. Converted to shares of ALL households: standpipe 0.25 x 0.51 = 12.75% -> PIPED per rubric (public taps/standpipes count as piped), excluded, and this is the single biggest reason Mayotte's unpiped share is far smaller than its 25%-without-running-water headline suggests; well/cistern 0.25 x 0.07 = 1.75% -> OtherUnpiped; river/bottled/other 0.25 x 0.05 = 1.25% -> OtherUnpiped; neighbours/family 0.25 x 0.04 = 1.00% -> PIPED per rubric ('piped to neighbour' is piped), excluded — this deliberately DIFFERS from the section file's suggested mapping, which put the neighbour share into Delivered. OtherUnpiped = 1.75 + 1.25 = 3.00%. Borehole left null: 'puits/citerne' merges dug wells with cisterns and INSEE does not separate drilled forages, so any Borehole share is a subset of the 3.00% rather than an addition to it (rubric rule 7). Delivered = 0: no tanker or vendor category appears anywhere in the breakdown. Packaged null: bottled is merged into the 'river/bottled/other' 5% and cannot be separated — the 1.25% assigned to OtherUnpiped therefore contains an unknown Packaged component. Also the 75% WITH running water are not broken down by source at all, so a household on its own borehole with running water is invisible. No urban/rural split published (breakdown is by housing type instead), so values applied to both.
bounds_notes: Unallocated: 'in-home storage' 18% of the 25% = 4.5% of all households, whose actual source INSEE does not identify — this is the largest single uncertainty in the row and could belong to any category. The listed sub-shares total 85% (51+18+7+5+4), leaving a further ~15% of the 25% (~3.75% of households) unaccounted for in the section file's transcription. So OtherUnpiped could plausibly be anywhere from 3.0% to ~11% if the storage and unaccounted groups are unpiped-sourced. Strong within-territory gradient: 61% of sheet-metal (tole) homes lack running water vs 6% of solid homes — if Mayotte is ever modelled by settlement type this matters far more than any urban/rural split. Trend note: standpipe reliance among the unconnected jumped from 18% (2013) to 51% (2024), i.e. the improvement has been toward public taps, not household connections.

source: ISEE, Recensement de la population 2019, open-data housing microdata RP2019NC_OD_logements.xlsx + variable dictionary (tabulated from raw microdata, n=90,813 main residences, CATL=1)
mapping_notes: The census variable is EAU = whether the dwelling has a 'point d'eau courante' (a running-water point). That is an ACCESS variable, not a source variable, and it cannot be converted into our categories in either direction. Two failures block a fill. (1) The 97.0% WITH a water point are not broken down by source at all — a dwelling fed by a tribal borehole, a rain tank or the municipal network all record EAU=1 identically, so we cannot read a Borehole or OtherUnpiped share out of the majority. (2) The 3.0% WITHOUT a water point in the dwelling are equally uninformative: the census does not code what they use, and the most likely answer for many of them is walking to a shared village tap — which is a standpipe, i.e. PIPED per the rubric. So 3.0% is not a value for OtherUnpiped and is not even a reliable ceiling on it. Filling OtherUnpiped = 3.0 was considered and rejected on exactly this reasoning. Recorded as bounds only.
bounds_notes: SOURCE QUALITY IS HIGH even though nothing is filled — the limitation is the questionnaire/definition, not the data. Figures available for later use if the variable is ever reinterpreted: 97.0% of main residences have a running-water point (88,114/90,813), 3.0% do not (2,699). By province — Iles Loyaute 92.1% / 7.9% none; Nord 95.6% / 4.4% none; Sud (incl. Noumea) 97.7% / 2.3% none. Province is a usable urban/rural proxy (Sud = urban-heavy; Nord + Iles Loyaute = rural), so if a fill is ever justified the urban/rural split would be roughly 2.3% vs 4.4-7.9%, not a single national number. Among dwellings WITH a water point: individual point 88.1%, collective/shared point 11.9% — the collective share is most likely shared taps/standpipes, which is piped per JMP and reinforces the reading that shared-tap use is widespread and that the 3.0% without a dwelling water point are not necessarily on natural sources. Data quality itself is excellent (raw official microdata); the limitation is the questionnaire, not the source.

source: Niue Statistics Office, 2022 Niue Census of Population and Dwellings Report, Tables 5.16 and 23 (main drinking source, n=513 households); PRIF Niue Country Profile for the pumped-groundwater description
mapping_notes: Census main-drinking-source table (2022): public piped 75.8%, bottled water 10.1%, household tank / naturally sourced rainwater 6.8%, other community source 7.0%, other 0.2%. Mapping: Packaged = 10.1 (bottled, described as growing in importance since 2017). OtherUnpiped = 6.8 (household rainwater tank). Borehole = 0 with evidence, not as a blank: Niue is a raised coral island whose groundwater lens is abstracted by the PUBLIC utility's electrically pumped bores and then reticulated, so household-level drilled wells are not a census category and are not described anywhere in the section - the groundwater dependence shows up in the piped 75.8%, not in our Borehole column. Delivered = 0: no tanker/cart/vendor category exists and none is described; bottled water is retail/imported and is already counted as Packaged. JUDGMENT CALL on 'other community source' 7.0%: assigned to PIPED and therefore EXCLUDED from our columns. Rationale - the census already has a separate household-level category for private tanks and natural sources, so 'community' denotes a shared supply distinct from the main public utility, i.e. a village-level scheme accessed at a tap; the rubric explicitly counts public taps, standpipes and village tap-houses as piped, and Niue has no surface water for a community source to be drawn from directly. If the 7.0% turns out to be shared rainwater cisterns drawn from directly rather than reticulated village schemes, OtherUnpiped would rise to 13.8 - the single biggest sensitivity in this row. The residual 'other' 0.2% is unspecified and was left unallocated rather than swept into OtherUnpiped. Census is reported by village with no urban/rural stratification (Niue is effectively a single rural population), so national values are applied to both columns per rubric rule 2.
bounds_notes: OtherUnpiped bound: 6.8 (as filled) to 13.8 (if 'other community source' 7.0% is direct-use shared catchment rather than a reticulated village scheme). Sum check: 10.1 + 0 + 0 + 6.8 + 82.8 piped (75.8 public + 7.0 other community) + 0.2 unallocated 'other' = 99.9, no overshoot. Report §2 master table lists the same four headline numbers and simply omits the 0.2% 'other'; a condensation, not a contradiction, so no discrepancy flag.

source: EurEau, 'Europe's Water in Figures - 2026 edition', Annex Fig.1: 100% connected to a public drinking-water network (2022-2024); Vewin (10 member utilities supply >17 million people, effectively the entire population); World Bank SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS 99.96% (2021)
mapping_notes: Evidence-based zeros (rubric rule 3). Three independent sources converge on ~100% public-network connection and the section notes the Netherlands has essentially no private household well tradition, so Borehole = 0. Delivered, OtherUnpiped and Packaged also set to 0 following the section's explicit statement 'Packaged/Delivered/OtherUnpiped ~ negligible/0'. Note the Packaged zero rests on that assertion, not on a bottled-water main-source statistic. Piped ~100% is excluded from our columns.

source: Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI/NIPH), 'Drinking water in Norway' (~90% of 4.6M served by approved/registered waterworks, ~10% / ~525,000 from waterworks not requiring approval, i.e. <50 people, including many private wells); FHI Vannverksregisteret 2023 report (1,390 systems serving >=50 residents cover ~88-89% of population)
mapping_notes: Category assignment is the weak link here, hence confidence low despite FHI being the correct regulator. FHI's sub-50-person tier is NOT broken out by source type - it mixes drilled wells (Borehole) with springs and surface intakes (OtherUnpiped). The full ~10% is placed in Borehole as a single best-supported category with OtherUnpiped/Delivered = 0 to avoid double-counting; the reliable quantity is Borehole+OtherUnpiped = 10%, and an unquantified share genuinely belongs in OtherUnpiped. 10.0 chosen as the low end of the 10-12% range (the ~10%/525,000 FHI statement is the concrete number; the 88-89% 2023 register coverage implies 11-12%). National figure applied to both strata although small/private supplies are rural-concentrated.
bounds_notes: Range across sources is 10-12% on small/unapproved supplies; the ~90% approved-waterworks figure is a 2014 baseline while the register figure is 2023.

source: EHINZ, Access to safe drinking-water, 2023 factsheet (2020/21 data, sourced from Taumata Arowai); corroborated by Taumata Arowai (~15% self-supply, >75,000 unregulated private supplies)
mapping_notes: Regulator-coverage proxy, not a household main-source question. 83.6% of the population (4.2M) is on registered drinking-water supplies; the residual 16.4% (~823,000 people) is described by EHINZ as being on 'small unregistered community supplies or self-supplies (rainwater tanks, bores)'. The source gives NO split between tanks and bores (rubric rule 4), and the section file explicitly rejects the commonly repeated '~10% rainwater' figure as having no traceable primary citation, so that number was NOT used to derive a split. In the absence of any split evidence the 16.4% was divided evenly: Borehole 8.2 / OtherUnpiped 8.2. This is an explicit assumption, not a measurement - if a tank/bore split is ever sourced, this row should be redone. The 16.4% is also a CEILING on self-supply for our four columns, because part of it is small unregistered COMMUNITY schemes, which the rubric counts as piped (reticulated village supplies / tap-houses) and which should be excluded; Taumata Arowai's tighter '~15% self-supply' figure suggests roughly 1-1.5 points of the 16.4% is community-scheme piped. The lower figure was not substituted because 16.4% is the primary, citable factsheet number. Packaged and Delivered are not quantified anywhere in the section and are left null (not 0 - no evidence either way). Only a national figure exists, so it is applied to both URBAN and RURAL per rubric rule 2; note this is known to be directionally wrong, since NZ self-supply is overwhelmingly rural, so URBAN 8.2/8.2 is an over-estimate and RURAL 8.2/8.2 an under-estimate.
bounds_notes: 16.4% is an upper bound on self-supply (includes unregistered community/reticulated schemes that belong in piped). Taumata Arowai's ~15% self-supply plus >75,000 unregulated private supplies is the tighter alternative. Sum check: piped/registered 83.6 + our 16.4 = 100.0, no overshoot.

source: USGS, 'Estimated water withdrawals and use in Puerto Rico, 2015' (domestic self-supplied population = ~4,708 people, all assumed groundwater, down from ~38,000 in 2010); system coverage from ASCE Puerto Rico Infrastructure Report Card 2019 (PRASA serves ~96-97% of ~3.3M; ~237 non-PRASA community systems serve ~3-4%, ~126,000-132,000 people).
mapping_notes: Borehole = 0.14: USGS self-supplied domestic population 4,708 / ~3.3M = 0.14%, and USGS assigns ALL self-supplied domestic withdrawal to groundwater, i.e. private wells -> Borehole. JUDGMENT CALL that changes the answer materially: the section file suggested OtherUnpiped ~3-4% for the non-PRASA community aqueducts, and I did NOT follow that. Those ~237 non-PRASA systems are piped community aqueducts delivering water into dwellings (many gravity-fed from springs); under JMP conventions the household's main source is 'piped', and the spring is the system's raw-water intake, not the household's collection point. Counting them as OtherUnpiped would misclassify ~130,000 piped-supplied people. With PRASA ~96-97% + non-PRASA ~3-4% both piped and USGS self-supply at 0.14%, the accounting closes at ~100%, leaving OtherUnpiped ~0 - written as 0 (rubric rule 3) rather than null, since USGS records no self-supplied domestic surface-water or rainwater population at all. Packaged/Delivered left null: no household main-drinking-source survey exists for PR (the Puerto Rico Community Survey has no water-source table), and bottled use post-Maria is certainly non-zero but wholly unquantified - a 0 there would be wrong. No urban/rural split published; non-PRASA is described as rural/mountainous, so the true rural Borehole/community-system share is higher than the national figure applied here.
bounds_notes: Non-PRASA community systems 3-4% of population (~126,000-132,000) - treated as piped, but if the model ever wants a 'not-utility-piped' resilience category they belong there, and many are gravity-fed springs (no electricity dependence), which is directly relevant to CIL resilience. Self-supplied domestic population fell from ~38,000 (2010, ~1%) to ~4,708 (2015), so the 0.14% is sensitive to the vintage chosen: a 2010 basis would give ~1.0.

source: ISPF, Recensement de la population 2022, housing module (candidate source — identified but NOT extracted)
